lead: A browser does not keep your HTML as text. It parses the tags and builds a tree of objects in memory called the Document Object Model, or DOM. Each tag becomes an element node, each run of text becomes a text node, and each attribute becomes an attribute node. JavaScript can walk this tree, read it and change it. Every change appears on screen at once. That is dynamic HTML: one loaded page that updates itself — a cart count, a live score, a filtered product list — without a full page reload.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 (HTML tags and forms), 3.1 and 3.3.

blocks.text: When the browser loads an HTML file it parses the tags from top to bottom. A tag becomes an element node; the text between tags becomes a text node; an attribute becomes an attribute node on its element. The result is the DOM, a tree with one root, document.
Under document is html. Its children are head and body. A node directly above another is its parent; nodes directly below are its children; nodes sharing a parent are siblings.

In the figure, document → html → body → h1#t and ul#items. The h1 has one text child, "Cart". The ul has one li child, and that li has the text child "Pen". White space between tags also makes text nodes; most tools ignore them.
The tree is live. Change a node and the browser repaints that part of the page. No HTTP request is needed.

Five methods find elements. document.getElementById('t') returns the one element with id t, or null. getElementsByClassName('red') and getElementsByTagName('li') return a live HTMLCollection. document.querySelector('#items li') returns the first match for any CSS selector. document.querySelectorAll('#items li') returns a NodeList of all matches.
A NodeList looks like an array: it has length and index access. It is not an array. It has no map, filter or push. Use Array.from(list) or [...list] when you need array methods.

Read text with el.textContent: it returns the text of the element and all descendants, tags removed. Set it to replace those children with one text node. Use el.innerHTML only for real HTML: it parses the string, discards existing children and their listeners, and inserts the resulting nodes. A script tag inserted this way does not execute, but event-handler attributes such as onerror and javascript: URLs do fire, so untrusted text is still an XSS risk.

For inputs read input.value. For attributes use el.getAttribute('href') and setAttribute('href', '/cart'). For classes use classList.add('red'), remove, toggle, contains. Inline styles use camelCase and units: el.style.backgroundColor = 'gold'; el.style.width = '200px'.

To add a node: create, fill, attach. const li = document.createElement('li') makes a detached element. li.textContent = 'Tea' gives it text. ul.appendChild(li) makes it the last child. ul.insertBefore(li, ref) puts it before the child ref. li.remove() deletes a node. ul.replaceChildren(a, b) replaces all children with a and b.

The browser also gives objects outside the document, together called the BOM (Browser Object Model). window is the global object. window.location.href = '/login' navigates to another page. history.back() goes to the previous page; history.length counts entries. navigator.userAgent is a string naming the browser. screen.width is display width in pixels. alert, confirm and prompt show dialogs. setTimeout(fn, 500) runs fn once after 500 ms; setInterval(fn, 1000) runs it every 1000 ms until clearInterval.
Session data usually lives on the server; the browser stores a cookie holding the session id and sends it with every request to that site. See Unit 4.

figure.caption: After the script: h1#t reads Cart: 2 items, and the first li Pen has class red. A new li Tea is appended under ul#items, so the li count goes from 1 to 2 (output 1 2).

spec.aria: DOM tree after the worked example: document contains html, whose body has h1 #t with text Cart: 2 items and ul #items with two li children, Pen marked class red and Tea new, count 1 to 2.

examples.question:
The page contains

Cart

and
  • Pen
. Write a script that (a) sets the heading text to 'Cart: 2 items', (b) appends a new li with text 'Tea', (c) gives the first li the class 'red', and (d) reports document.querySelectorAll('#items li').length before and after step (b). Show the output.
steps: Before any change, document.querySelectorAll('#items li') matches one li (Pen). Length = 1.
document.getElementById('t') finds h1#t. Setting .textContent = 'Cart: 2 items' replaces its text child. The heading now reads Cart: 2 items.
document.createElement('li') creates a detached li. Setting .textContent = 'Tea' gives it one text node.
document.getElementById('items').appendChild(li) inserts that li as the second child of ul#items. The count becomes 2.
document.querySelector('#items li') returns the first match, the Pen li. .classList.add('red') adds class red to it. The count stays 2.
The count is read at the end; the class change in step (c) does not add or remove li elements, so it is still 2. The two saved counts print as 1 2.
examples.answer: Before appending, querySelectorAll('#items li').length is 1; after appending it is 2.

traps: innerHTML with user text opens an XSS hole and destroys listeners inside the element. Use textContent for plain text.
querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList; getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that changes as the page changes.
getElementById returns null when no element matches. Reading .textContent on null throws a TypeError.
style.width = 200 fails silently; CSS lengths need a unit string such as '200px'.
appendChild on a node already in the document moves it, it does not copy it. Use cloneNode(true) to copy.

quiz.q: What is the DOM and what is its root node?
quiz.a: The DOM is the browser's tree of nodes built from HTML. Its root is the document node.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between textContent and innerHTML when setting an element's content.
quiz.a: textContent treats the string as plain text and inserts one text node. innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so tags become elements; an inserted script tag does not itself run, but inline handlers such as onerror do, so untrusted text is dangerous.

quiz.q: Given a ul element with id 'list' containing two li elements with text A and B, write JavaScript that changes the text of the second li to C and adds class done to it.
quiz.a: const second = document.querySelectorAll('#list li')[1]; second.textContent = 'C'; second.classList.add('done');

quiz.q: A NodeList from querySelectorAll is called static, while an HTMLCollection from getElementsByClassName is called live. Explain what happens to each after a new matching li is appended, and why this matters in a loop.
quiz.a: The static NodeList keeps its old length and old element references. The live HTMLCollection updates to include the new li. In a loop that appends matching items, a live collection can run forever or skip items; copy it to an array first.

quiz.q: Write the three lines that create an li with text 'Tea' and append it to ul#items.
Name three BOM objects and one method or property of each.
A student sets box.innerHTML = comment from a user. Give two problems this causes.
quiz.a: It allows XSS: user text can inject a script or an onerror handler. It also destroys the element's existing children and their event listeners.

beyond: Not for the exam. Frameworks such as React keep a virtual DOM and diff it before touching the real tree (see Unit 5). The Shadow DOM hides a subtree inside a component so outside CSS cannot reach it. MutationObserver reports additions and removals in the DOM. Web components combine custom elements, templates and shadow DOM. Search for 'Shadow DOM', 'MutationObserver' and 'web components MDN'.
